title: Evaluating the Impact of Temperature and Instruction Strategies on Hallucination in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive generative and reasoning abilities, yet their tendency to produce factually incorrect or fabricated information—so-called hallucinations—remains a key limitation. This study systematically examines how temperature and system instruction strategies affect hallucination behavior in open-source LLMs executed through the Ollama framework. Three representative models—Gemma 2B, Mistral 7B Instruct, and Phi-3 Mini—were evaluated on the TruthfulQA benchmark using zero-shot, few-shot, and “say-I-don’t-know” prompting paradigms. Performance was measured through exact match, token-level F1, semantic similarity, and embedding-based similarity metrics. Two-way ANOVA and3 Tukey post-hoc analyses revealed that system instruction significantly influenced factual accuracy across all models, while temperature effects were comparatively minor. Few-shot prompting achieved the highest mean F1 score (0.1889), indicating that example conditioning effectively constrained hallucinations. Conversely, “say-I-don’t-know” prompts increased semantic alignment but reduced precision, suggesting a conservative refusal bias. Embedding-based similarity analyses confirmed higher semantic consistency for zero-shot responses. The results highlight that prompt design exerts a stronger and more interpretable influence on hallucination than sampling stochasticity, offering practical guidance for improving the factual reliability of open-source LLMs.

claims.text: Few-shot prompting achieved the highest mean F1 score of 0.1889 among the evaluated system instruction strategies on TruthfulQA.
Zero-shot prompting achieved a higher Sentence Transformer embedding similarity score (mean 0.673) than few-shot (0.646) and say-IDK (0.645) strategies.
System instruction strategy had a statistically significant main effect on factual accuracy and semantic similarity metrics across all evaluated models.
Decoding temperature had a smaller effect size on model accuracy and semantic metrics compared to system instruction strategy.
Increasing decoding temperature from 0.0 to 0.7 resulted in slight performance declines across factual and semantic alignment metrics.
There was no statistically significant interaction effect between decoding temperature and system instruction strategy.

limitations.text: The evaluation was restricted to lightweight open-source models (Gemma 2B, Mistral 7B Instruct, Phi-3 Mini) evaluated on a single benchmark (TruthfulQA).
The study intentionally excluded temperature settings above 0.7, focusing only on a low-to-moderate decoding regime.
Knowledge overshadowing causes dominant knowledge representations to suppress less frequent knowledge during generation, resulting in factual hallucinations.

future_work.text: Assess the generalizability of temperature and instruction strategy effects across larger models, alternative benchmarks, and real-world deployment settings.
Extend evaluation to multimodal tasks, domain-specific applications, and adaptive decoding or instruction strategies.

methodologies.name: Ollama-based Multi-Factor Hallucination Evaluation Protocol
methodologies.description: A experimental pipeline that evaluates open-source LLMs on TruthfulQA across combinations of decoding temperatures and instruction strategies using lexical and sentence-embedding similarity metrics.
